{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mn-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"612abd1c480ff7fe6c41f2bacaffb887aae736c8e82a725c94ff57cc798e2716","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mn-class-d:lineage:55","source_registry_sha256":"960e2daa314aff60b32f5124e42324d79615ce2a3ea953a336216b4593c0c910","source_liveness_sha256":"0b70283fc58b1f8ea1822994a92e3ce7ff4b722004376a9cd819180969b6fe1e"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driving privileges: driving record, suspension, revocation, limited license and cancellation","heading":"C — Your driving privileges: the driving record, how a license is withdrawn, grounds for suspension, grounds for revocation, reinstatement, the limited license, cancellation and commercial disqualification","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Your driving privileges: the driving record, how a license is withdrawn, grounds for suspension, grounds for revocation, reinstatement, the limited license, cancellation and commercial disqualification
Knowledge domain: why driving in Minnesota is a privilege that can be withdrawn, the three ways DPS withdraws a license, what actions lead to suspension, revocation or cancellation, how privileges are reinstated, and what a limited license allows.

FACT_ID: sec13-F01 | anchor: A01
Driving in Minnesota is a privilege that you can lose by breaking certain laws or failing to meet certain requirements. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F02 | anchor: A01
DVS keeps a record of your driving that includes violations in Minnesota and in other states, and serious or repeated violations can lead to losing your privilege or to limits on where, when and what you may drive. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F03 | anchor: A01
A license can be withdrawn in three ways: suspension, revocation or cancellation, and DPS then mails a notice of withdrawal listing the reinstatement requirements. [A01]
Why it matters: the three withdrawal types are a likely test item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F04 | anchor: A01
Repeatedly breaking traffic laws, or a conviction for a violation that contributed to a crash causing death, injury or serious property damage, can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F05 | anchor: A01
Letting anyone else use your license or permit is illegal, and using or lending a license for an illegal act can bring a suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F06 | anchor: A01
A traffic offense committed in another state can lead to suspension if it would be grounds for suspension in Minnesota. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F07 | anchor: A01
A court finding that you are legally unfit to drive, or failing to report a medical condition that would cancel your privileges, can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F08 | anchor: A01
Failing to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights within five years of an earlier conviction for the same offense can lead to suspension. [A01]
Why it matters: the five-year repeat window is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F09 | anchor: A01
Having a fake or altered license, applying fraudulently for a license or ID card, or taking any part of the license exam for someone else can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F10 | anchor: A01
Falsely identifying yourself to a police officer can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F11 | anchor: A01
Failing to appear in court or to pay a fine for a motor vehicle violation when required, or a misdemeanor conviction under Minnesota traffic law, can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F12 | anchor: A01
Failing to pay court-ordered child support can lead to a license suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F13 | anchor: A01
Using or lending a license, permit or ID card to buy tobacco for someone under 18 or alcohol for someone under 21 can lead to suspension. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F14 | anchor: A01
A driver under 21 whom a court finds drove while or after consuming alcohol can have their license suspended. [A01]
Why it matters: the under-twenty-one alcohol rule is a likely test item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec13-F15 | anchor: A02
Paying a state or license agent fee with a bad check brings a suspension that is lifted once the check and related fees are fully paid. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F16 | anchor: A02
A conviction for theft of gasoline can lead to suspension. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F17 | anchor: A02
After a suspension ends, privileges may be reinstated once all requirements are met, including paying the reinstatement fee, and you must apply for a new license if it expired or your name or address changed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F18 | anchor: A02
Refusing a test for alcohol or a controlled substance, or failing that test, can lead to revocation. [A02]
Why it matters: test refusal leads to revocation, not just suspension.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F19 | anchor: A02
A conviction for driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol, or for manslaughter or another crime committed while driving, can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F20 | anchor: A02
A conviction for a felony in which a motor vehicle was used can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F21 | anchor: A02
A conviction for driving faster than 100 mph can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F22 | anchor: A02
A conviction for fleeing a police officer can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F23 | anchor: A02
Failing to stop, identify yourself and give aid after a crash, especially one causing death or injury, can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F24 | anchor: A02
Lying under oath, signing a false legal document about a vehicle's ownership or operation, or making a false statement to DPS about it can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F25 | anchor: A02
Pleading guilty or forfeiting bail for three violations in one year of Minnesota traffic laws or ordinances that require a jail sentence on conviction can lead to revocation. [A02]
Why it matters: three jailable violations in a year is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F26 | anchor: A02
Driving a vehicle you know lacks no-fault insurance, or owning an uninsured vehicle and knowingly driving it or letting others drive it, can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F27 | anchor: A02
A gross misdemeanor conviction for failing to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F28 | anchor: A02
A conviction for selling or possessing a controlled substance while operating a motor vehicle can lead to revocation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F29 | anchor: A02
After a revocation period ends you must meet every requirement on the withdrawal notice, show proper identification at the written or road test, and apply for a new license once testing is complete. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec13-F30 | anchor: A03
A limited license may be issued to some drivers whose privileges are revoked or suspended, but only after they meet requirements that include any mandatory waiting period. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec13-F31 | anchor: A03
A limited license allows travel only to and from work, chemical dependency treatment or counseling, and a post-secondary school where you are enrolled, plus driving household dependents for medical, educational or nutritional needs. [A03]
Why it matters: limited license purposes are a likely test item.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec13-F32 | anchor: A03
A license may be canceled when you have no legal right to it, for example if a mental or physical disability makes you unable to drive safely or you fail a test DPS legally requests. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec13-F33 | anchor: A03
Giving false or misleading information on a license application brings a cancellation of 60 days or until the correct information is provided, whichever is longer. [A03]
Why it matters: the false application cancellation length is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec13-F34 | anchor: A03
A license may also be canceled when cancellation is a legal punishment for a crime, or when you do not qualify for a license under Minnesota law. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0093]

Misconceptions: refusing an alcohol test is not a way to avoid penalties, because refusal itself can bring revocation; a limited license does not restore general driving; suspension, revocation and cancellation are different actions with different grounds; a bad-check suspension ends only when everything is paid.
Mnemonics: suspend for repeats, money and paperwork, revoke for alcohol, speed over one hundred, fleeing and serious crimes, cancel when you never had the right; limited means work, treatment, school and dependents.
Glossary: suspension means a temporary withdrawal of driving privileges; revocation means a withdrawal that ends only after a period and full reinstatement requirements including a new license; cancellation means withdrawal because you have no legal right to the license; limited license means a restricted license for specific trips; reinstatement means getting driving privileges back after meeting the listed requirements.
Dynamic facts: the driving record website named in the chapter can change; recheck it against an official DVS source before each release.
